title: Concurrency and Resource Management
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of concurrency and resource management in a FastAPI application.
Apply or interpret one example related to concurrent request handling.
Identify one limitation or failure case and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson covers concurrency and resource management within asynchronous programming and concurrency. Use the supplied syllabus topics as the coverage checklist, then connect them to the worked example and the verification task.
content.why_it_matters: You will use concurrency and resource management to build APIs whose contracts and behavior are understandable to both clients and maintainers. The practical aim is resource lifecycle, cancellation, concurrency limits and observable I/O behavior.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Concurrency and Resource Management matters because it is part of asynchronous programming and concurrency. In practice, focus on resource lifecycle, cancellation, concurrency limits and observable I/O behavior. A framework feature only helps when its assumptions match the application; keep input validation, business policy and side effects distinguishable.

items.title: Concurrent request handling
items.text: For concurrent request handling, identify which operation waits on I/O, which resources remain open, and what happens on timeout or disconnect. Async syntax does not make CPU-bound work faster or durable background jobs reliable by itself.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Concurrency and Resource Management
content_blocks.code:
import asyncio

async def fetch_one(name: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0)  # stand-in for non-blocking I/O
    return name

async def main():
    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch_one("A"), fetch_one("B"))
    print(results)
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run with asyncio.run(main()) in a standalone Python script. Async helps I/O concurrency; it does not make CPU-heavy code automatically faster.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For read-only examples, no reset is needed. For any example that writes state, use a disposable local database/test fixture; record the starting state and clean up only lab data. Never use production credentials or real personal data.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a code fragment without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Installed versions, imported types, application structure and external services affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: State assumptions; check the versioned official docs; run a minimal local test and add one failure case.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one happy-path response as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid input, permissions, concurrency, timeouts and cleanup are not exercised by a single request.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused normal and negative tests and record exact expected status/body.

common_mistakes.why: Even short examples may mutate records, reveal data or affect availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic inputs and a disposable environment; review security, cleanup and rollback before promotion.
